Infrastructure: servers and providers, node bootstrap, cloud servers, the fleet, database and storage servers and what is inside them, adoption from other panels, patching, quotas and billing status.

| At a glance          |                                                                                                                          |
| -------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| **Endpoint**         | `https://g8deck.app/mcp/platform`                                                                                        |
| **Server name**      | `g8deck-platform`                                                                                                        |
| **Who can reach it** | Ops only. Reaching it needs `mcp.access.platform`, which no customer role holds.                                         |
| **Authentication**   | A personal access token (`Authorization: Bearer …`) or OAuth 2.1 sign-in — see [Connect an AI client](/docs/mcp/connect) |
| **Route limit**      | 30 requests per minute                                                                                                   |
| **Tools**            | 62 — 30 read, 25 write, 7 destroy                                                                                        |

Every tool needs a token carrying its tier: `mcp:read`, `mcp:write` or `mcp:destroy`, each tier including the ones before it. On top of the route limit, each caller gets 60 read, 20 write and 5 destroy calls a minute. Your role decides which tools answer at all; a tool you can see but lack the permission for answers `permission_denied` and names the permission. Secret and credential values never cross this boundary — tools take them inbound and report key names only.

## What the client is told

The server sends these instructions to every AI client that connects, before any tool is called. They are reproduced verbatim because they carry the reading rules that change what an answer means.

<details class="instructions">
<summary>Server instructions</summary>

```text
G8Deck platform server — infrastructure providers, node bootstrap, quotas and control-plane health. Ops-only.

Conventions:
- Call `whoami` first. Reaching this server needs `mcp.access.platform`, which customers do not have.
- Providers are identified by uuid; they have no slug. Every tool accepts an optional `organization` and echoes the one it used.
- **Credential values never cross this boundary** — only which credential fields are set. The SSH host key fingerprint IS returned: it is trust state to compare, not a secret to present.
- **Check simulated capabilities before trusting a result.** A simulated capability is a declared fake: steps depending on it record Skipped with a reason instead of reporting success. `list-infra-providers` and `get-infra-provider` both report them.
- `update-infra-provider` is the only write that touches a provider *row*, and it is bookkeeping only: name, location, active flag and the protection lock. Credentials and `type` are not editable here — credential values never cross this boundary — and the lock may be added but never removed over MCP. It takes final values, not deltas: omitted fields are left alone, and the response names every field that actually moved.
- `delete-infra-provider` removes a provider row. **It destroys no machine.** What it removes is the credential, so a host adopted over SSH becomes unreachable rather than gone — it keeps running and keeps billing until its own hosting provider deletes it. It needs `mcp:destroy` and the name retyped, and it is refused for the control plane and for any provider that still has live deployments, node pools, managed nodes or bootstrap history. Tear those down first; a deployment left without its provider cannot be torn down through G8Deck at all.
- **`list-nodes` and `list-managed-nodes` are different questions.** `list-nodes` reports the per-deployment placements a provisioning run created; `list-managed-nodes` reports the machines G8Deck can actually reach — the fleet. A teardown works on the second. `retire-managed-node` withdraws one: it uninstalls nothing and shuts nothing down, so the host keeps running and keeps billing; it is refused for the control plane, keeps the bootstrap history, and confirms on the SSH **host address** rather than the hostname, which can be blank or shared.
- **A database server is a daemon on a node, not a machine.** `list-database-servers` reports the ones G8Deck administers, and a null `node` means the machine underneath is already retired — a stale record that administers nothing (`orphaned: true` lists exactly those). `withdraw-database-server` removes that record and discards the stored admin credential; it drops no data and stops no bill, because the machine is what costs money. It confirms on the **endpoint** (`host:port`), never the engine name — every PostgreSQL server is called PostgreSQL.
- **Working INSIDE a database server** is `list-managed-databases` (databases, login roles and every grant in one read) plus six writes. Everything is queued: a record is written with status `pending`, the daemon converges after, and `failed` carries the daemon's own reason — so read the state back rather than assuming the call settled it. Names are validated against the server's ENGINE, not a generic rule (`mysql` is the account table on MySQL and an ordinary name on PostgreSQL; `root` and `postgres` are each sacred on one family), and a dropped name **stays reserved** on its server, so "already exists" can name something nobody can see any more. **`create-database-user` generates the password and never returns it** — reveal it on the server's page, behind `database-servers.reveal.credentials`, where the reveal is audited. There is **one privilege per (database, user) pair**: `grant-database-access` REPLACES what the role held rather than adding to it, and the response names what it replaced. `revoke-database-access` removes a grant and is `mcp:write`, not destructive — it deletes no data and drops no role — while `drop-managed-database` (which **deletes the data**) and `drop-database-user` (which does not, but cuts off everything connecting as that role) both need `mcp:destroy` and the name or username retyped. Those repeat across *servers* and are unique on the one you just named, which is what makes them a lock rather than ceremony.
- **PostgreSQL extensions are per DATABASE; the package that provides one is per SERVER.** `list-database-extensions` keeps three facts apart — the catalogue G8Deck offers, what the DAEMON can load (`available`, read from the machine, with `available_error` when nobody could look: an empty list is not the same answer), and what is enabled in each database. `enable-database-extension` does both halves in order and reports which refused. `disable-database-extension` **never passes CASCADE and takes no argument that would** — the daemon refuses while any column still uses the type, that refusal IS the feature, and it reaches the record verbatim rather than translated, because CASCADE would make the drop succeed by deleting the customer's columns. On the RHEL family an enable refuses with a reason instead of naming a PGDG package: PGDG's build belongs to PGDG's own PostgreSQL installation and the AppStream daemon would never read it, so relay that refusal rather than reading it as a generic failure.
- **PostgreSQL replication (Stage 1: replicas + manual promotion; nothing fails over on its own).** `get-database-cluster` reads any member's cluster — roles, health and a replication reading that keeps never-probed, could-not-determine, unreachable and a real state apart. `add-database-replica` queues a streaming replica on another bootstrapped node (PostgreSQL only; the target's data directory is replaced by a base backup, and a daemon holding anything the cluster does not account for is refused). `promote-database-replica` (mcp:destroy, endpoint retyped) stops the old primary FIRST and refuses to continue if it cannot, unless `accept_data_loss` — it also refuses on any sign of lost writes without that flag. Afterwards records move to the new primary and applications get the new DB_HOST on their NEXT DEPLOY; the old primary and other replicas read `failed` until rebuilt (re-running their setup rebuilds them as replicas). Databases, users and attachments always resolve to the primary; creating a database or user on a replica is refused.
- `list-storage-buckets` reports the organisation's managed buckets: which server each sits on, its status, its quotas, how many keys are granted onto it, and which deployment and application (if any) is attached. **A bucket with no attachment is not spare capacity** — it still holds every object ever written to it, because detaching an application on the ops server deletes no data. Access key secrets do not cross this boundary, and neither do access key ids: half a credential is still a credential.
- **A storage server can be a Garage cluster.** `get-storage-cluster` reads its node set (the primary plus additional members), the replication factor, the S3 backends and a LIVE health reading — `unknown` means the reading could not be taken, never down; `absent` means the daemon does not know that node. `add-storage-member` queues a node into the cluster (installed with the cluster's existing secret, RPC opened between members only, given a layout role, data rebalanced onto it). `remove-storage-member` takes one out of the layout (`mcp:destroy`, confirms on the member's SSH host address) and is REFUSED when fewer nodes than the replication factor would remain; it stops nothing on the removed machine, which keeps running and billing. The replication factor is fixed at setup (1 or 3; 3 needs three nodes).
- `read-node-logs` reads a **machine's own** logs — nginx, syslog, the journal, the agent, and every native workload's log files. That is a different question from `get-deployment-logs`, which reports what one deployment printed: a server carrying no deployment at all, the control plane included, is readable only here, and until this tool existed debugging G8Deck's own 500 meant leaving the product. The source is a **fixed whitelist** and there is deliberately no path and no command parameter — a log tool that takes a path is arbitrary file read across the whole fleet behind nothing but a read permission, and one that takes a command is worse. `unit` is the only free text that reaches a machine, and it is bounded to a systemd unit name. Called without a `source` it lists the sources rather than guessing, because the wrong log read as the right one sends an investigation somewhere confident and wrong.
- **Adoption is four separate acts, and each is usable on its own**: sweep a machine another panel runs (`run-adoption-sweep`), read what is on it (`get-adoption-source`), decide what comes across (`decide-adoption-item`), register the machine (`adopt-discovered-server`). None of them changes anything on the customer's server — the sweep's adapter interface has no write methods, and adopting is a login check, `hostname` and `/etc/os-release`. **Adopting migrates nothing**: the old panel keeps serving, keeps its cron and keeps renewing certificates until a cutover moves each application, which is not built yet.
- **Read the coexistence risks before planning anything.** They are ordered by how QUIETLY each fails, not by severity: two schedulers double-fire every job and two ACME clients exhaust a rate limit, both with no error at all, while a duplicate php-fpm socket fails loudly and is therefore the safer one. A silent hazard is what actually causes the incident.
- **A remote database is a reference, not a migration** — the application keeps pointing at it. `decide-adoption-item` refuses to mark one adopt, because adopt there means move the data. On the first fleet swept this single rule removed all data risk from three of seven applications.
- **Discovery reports which environment keys exist, never their values.** A sweep that stored them would move the customer's secrets into our logs and job payloads; values are read once, later, by `import-adoption-env` — which writes them straight into the encrypted column and reports key names and verbs, never a value. It skips what the NEW machine owns (`DB_*`, `REDIS_*`, `APP_KEY`, `APP_URL`) and what the recipe manages in production (`APP_ENV`, `APP_DEBUG`); `carry` brings one across deliberately, which is how `APP_KEY` must travel, since a fresh key cannot read a single encrypted column.
- **Moving the DATA is `migrate-adoption-data`** (dry_run by default): the application's MySQL/MariaDB database (dumped with its own .env credentials, imported into the database `attach-application-database` made) and named paths relative to its root, into the application's shared/ tree. A run REPLACES the target and fails on any row-count or file-count mismatch; a second run is the final sync, with `put_source_in_maintenance: true`. Read progress with `get-adoption-data-migration`. Names and counts only — never a credential or a row.
- **An undecided item is not an adopted one.** Undecided is the default and must stay it: three of ten applications on the pilot fleet were Skip — one dead, two replaced by a rewrite — so silence must never read as consent.
- `trust-host-key` is the only way to move a pinned SSH host key, and it never clears one. A rebuilt machine presents a new key and every connection then fails closed; pass the fingerprint you mean to trust and it is compared against what the host presents before anything is stored. Node rows at the same address are re-pinned in the same call, because a node's pin wins over its provider's.
- `upgrade-fleet` brings behind servers up to the current node stack **one at a time**, stopping at the first failure so the rest are untouched. It is never simultaneous and that is not a throttle: a sweep that upgraded every node at once would find out about a bad stack revision on all of them together. Only the difference is applied, never a re-bootstrap. Calling it while a sweep is running reports that sweep rather than starting a second, so it is safe to poll. **Adopted servers are excluded and always will be** — an adopted machine carries no G8Deck stack to diff against, so nothing a fleet upgrade installs reaches it; the response names each excluded machine with its reason, and those machines are the operator's own to bring forward from their server page.
- `patch-fleet` is a different operation from `upgrade-fleet`: it moves the packages **already installed** for one target (php, node, python, nginx, mysql, mariadb, postgresql, redis, valkey, container-runtime, os-security) to the newest build their repository carries — a patch release for a CVE, never a new install and never a major/minor change. A **canary** goes first — one server per organisation (at least one application, no production application, fewest applications; a canary that proves nothing — nothing-installed or no_applications — hands the role to the next server with an application), patched and health-checked alone — and the rest are patched **in parallel** once it is healthy, because waiting machine-by-machine leaves the rest exposed while apt cannot downgrade a bad patch. A failed canary or failures on two servers **halt** the run (`halted`, `halted_reason`, the rest `skipped`); an application that could not be probed is `could_not_probe`, never a pass and never a failure (unless its systemd units are down, which is `failed_health`); a canary in that state still fans out and the run reports `canary_unverified`. `canary: false` is the emergency opt-out. php-fpm and nginx reload gracefully by default; database, cache, container-runtime, node and python restarts happen only with `restart: true`, otherwise the result is `restart_pending` and the old build keeps running. Read each server's `after` versions and `stale` processes against the advisory — that is the evidence, not the exit code. Adopted, protected and unreachable servers are excluded by name; the control plane only with `include_control_plane: true` (or `php artisan g8deck:patch` on its host), where its own worker units are held, never restarted.
- `restart-pending` acts on a `restart_pending` result: with no `nodes` it lists what still runs the old build per server (`units`, `stale`, the control plane's `held` units, the expected `interruption`); with `nodes` it restarts **exactly** the units the patch recorded as pending — health-checked before and after like a patch, outcome written back on the run result (`restarted` / `failed_health` / `failed`) and audited with you as approver. `schedule: true` queues it for the organisation's next maintenance window; `cancel: true` cancels a scheduled one. Held units are never restarted.
- **Patching is consented once, by policy.** `get-patch-policy` reads the organisation's policy — `automatic` (the default), `notify_only` or `manual`, the maintenance window in the organisation's timezone, `allow_disruptive_restarts` — and each server's override and effective mode (the stricter of the two). `set-patch-policy` (organisation administrator) changes it; moving to notify_only or manual, for the organisation or one server, is refused without `acknowledge_risk: true`, and the acknowledgement is audited. In automatic mode the scheduler patches inside the window through `patch-fleet`'s canary and halt, one target at a time per organisation, never the control plane and never an adopted server. A superadmin may call `patch-fleet` with `organization: "*"` for a platform-wide emergency: one run per organisation, each audited on its own trail.
- **Advisories are matched, not assumed.** `publish-advisory` (ops, `mcp.access.cross-tenant`; `dry_run` first) records an advisory per patch target with per-branch ranges and tells every organisation with an exposed server, in its policy's words; a critical one in automatic mode patches now, outside the window, graceful only. Exposure is read from the versions patch runs RECORDED and has four states — exposed, fixed, not_exploitable_here (`assess-advisory`, with a reason, audited) and unknown, which is never fixed. `get-advisory-exposure` lists every server with what it was judged on and whether the scheduler will patch it; `list-advisories` summarises per organisation and lists critical advisories still exposed 24h after notice.
- **Adding a server** is one of two tools, both organisation-administrator and both queued (poll `get-bootstrap-job`). `create-cloud-server` creates a machine at the organisation's connected cloud account — it SPENDS MONEY, is refused before the spend when the plan has no room, and only accepts an image a setup template can bootstrap. `register-ssh-server` records a machine that already exists, in two calls: the first records nothing and returns the SSH host key fingerprint; the second repeats the arguments with that fingerprint, which must match what the host presents before the row is written with the key pinned and the bootstrap queued. It never trusts on first use, and it refuses this control plane's own address.
- `create-git-credential` stores an HTTPS token for one git host, INBOUND ONLY; `list-git-credentials` reports which hosts have one, never the token. SSH repository URLs use a per-application deploy key instead, generated by G8Deck — only its public half is ever shown.
- `start-node-bootstrap` runs with the provider's decrypted credentials against the host you name. The provider must belong to your organisation — naming another tenant's is refused, not merely audited.
- The template's `os_type` is a dropdown someone picked; the bootstrap detects the real OS from /etc/os-release and fails on a family mismatch BEFORE the credential rotation, so a wrong template costs nothing.
- Billing: "node" means a VM on a hypervisor but a container on Docker, so `get-billable-hosts` reads the stored per-cluster count rather than counting node rows. An unreachable cluster keeps its last known count — an outage is not a cluster that shrank to zero.
- Quotas use 0 to mean "does not constrain at this scope", never "zero allowed".
- `system-health` answers "is anything going to run at all": queue depth, failed jobs, the scheduler heartbeat and the mail transport actually in force.
```

</details>

## Read tools

### `whoami`

<p class="tool-meta">Tier <code>mcp:read</code></p>

Report who you are: identity, roles, which MCP servers you may reach, your token's abilities, the organisations you can address and which one is used when you omit the `organization` argument. Call this first.

Takes no parameters.

### `list-infra-providers`

<p class="tool-meta">Tier <code>mcp:read</code> · permission <code>infra-providers.view.list</code></p>

Infrastructure providers in an organisation: type, health and — the part that matters — which of each provider's capabilities are SIMULATED. A simulated capability reports success without touching anything real. `orphaned: true` marks a provider that had a machine and has none now — it reaches nothing, and is the stale record retire-managed-node's remove_connection option clears.

| Parameter      | Type    | Description                                                                                                                                   |
| -------------- | ------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `organization` | string  | Organisation uuid or slug. Omit to use your default organisation.                                                                             |
| `orphaned`     | boolean | Only providers that had a machine and have none now — stale rows left behind when a machine was retired without also removing the connection. |

### `get-infra-provider`

<p class="tool-meta">Tier <code>mcp:read</code> · permission <code>infra-providers.view.list</code></p>

One provider in full: capabilities (real vs simulated), node pools, billing model and which credential FIELDS are configured. Credential values never cross this boundary; the SSH host key fingerprint does, because it is trust state to compare rather than a secret to present.

| Parameter                                    | Type   | Description                                                       |
| -------------------------------------------- | ------ | ----------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `provider` <span class="req">required</span> | string | Provider uuid. Providers have no slug.                            |
| `organization`                               | string | Organisation uuid or slug. Omit to use your default organisation. |

### `list-node-pools`

<p class="tool-meta">Tier <code>mcp:read</code> · permission <code>infra-providers.view.list</code></p>

Node pools across this organisation's providers, with their per-node shape.

| Parameter      | Type   | Description                                                       |
| -------------- | ------ | ----------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `organization` | string | Organisation uuid or slug. Omit to use your default organisation. |

### `list-nodes`

<p class="tool-meta">Tier <code>mcp:read</code> · permission <code>deployments.view.list</code></p>

Every node across the organisation's deployments. Note that "node" means different things per provider — a VM on a hypervisor, a container on Docker, a service on Swarm — which is why billing does not simply count these rows.

| Parameter      | Type    | Description                                                       |
| -------------- | ------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `deployment`   | string  | Deployment uuid or slug.                                          |
| `organization` | string  | Organisation uuid or slug. Omit to use your default organisation. |
| `page`         | integer | Page number, starting at 1.                                       |
| `per_page`     | integer | Results per page, 1-100 (default 20).                             |

### `list-managed-nodes`

<p class="tool-meta">Tier <code>mcp:read</code> · permission <code>infra-providers.view.list</code></p>

The machines G8Deck can reach: every server bootstrapped or adopted into this organisation, with its address, OS, stack state (current / behind / adopted) and whether it is protected. `stack_state: behind` is what upgrade-fleet acts on; `adopted` is a third answer, not a flavour of behind — an adopted machine carries no G8Deck stack to compare against and a fleet upgrade structurally cannot reach it. This is the fleet — distinct from list-nodes, which reports the per-deployment placements a provisioning run created. Credentials never cross this boundary; the SSH host key fingerprint does, because it is trust state to compare.

| Parameter      | Type    | Description                                                       |
| -------------- | ------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `provider`     | string  | Only nodes belonging to this provider uuid.                       |
| `organization` | string  | Organisation uuid or slug. Omit to use your default organisation. |
| `page`         | integer | Page number, starting at 1.                                       |
| `per_page`     | integer | Results per page, 1-100 (default 20).                             |

### `read-node-logs`

<p class="tool-meta">Tier <code>mcp:read</code> · permission <code>infra-providers.view.list</code></p>

Tail one log source off a machine in the fleet — the journal (optionally one systemd unit), nginx error or access, syslog, the G8Deck agent log, or every native workload's own log files. This is the machine's own logs, as opposed to get-deployment-logs, which reports what one deployment printed: a server carrying no deployment at all, the control plane included, is only readable here. The source is a fixed whitelist; there is no path or command parameter. Output is redacted by default; unmasked output requires deployments.view.logs-raw. Call without a source to list what can be read.

| Parameter                                | Type    | Description                                                                                                             |
| ---------------------------------------- | ------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `node` <span class="req">required</span> | string  | Managed node uuid, from list-managed-nodes.                                                                             |
| `source`                                 | string  | Which log to read. Omit to list the sources and what each one is.                                                       |
| `unit`                                   | string  | Systemd unit to narrow the journal to, e.g. nginx.service or g8deck-app-php-fpm.service. Ignored by every other source. |
| `lines`                                  | integer | How many lines to tail, 1-1000 (default 200).                                                                           |
| `raw`                                    | boolean | Request unmasked output. Requires deployments.view.logs-raw; otherwise output stays redacted and the response says so.  |
| `organization`                           | string  | Organisation uuid or slug. Omit to use your default organisation.                                                       |

### `list-adoption-sources`

<p class="tool-meta">Tier <code>mcp:read</code> · permission <code>migration-sources.view.list</code></p>

Servers being inventoried ahead of adoption — a machine another control panel (RunCloud, cPanel, plain nginx) still administers. Reports what each sweep concluded and how far the decisions have got. A FAILED sweep is not an empty machine: it carries the reason it could not look, which is a different answer from "nothing is there".

| Parameter      | Type    | Description                                                            |
| -------------- | ------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `status`       | string  | Only sources in this status: pending, discovering, discovered, failed. |
| `organization` | string  | Organisation uuid or slug. Omit to use your default organisation.      |
| `page`         | integer | Page number, starting at 1.                                            |
| `per_page`     | integer | Results per page, 1-100 (default 20).                                  |

### `get-adoption-source`

<p class="tool-meta">Tier <code>mcp:read</code> · permission <code>migration-sources.view.list</code></p>

One inventoried server in full: every application with its runtime, domains, source repository and decision; every database classified local or remote; every scheduled job and worker; and the coexistence hazards, ordered by how QUIETLY each fails rather than by severity. For an application marked Adopt it also returns the reconciliation plan — what was found beside what G8Deck would create. Environment variable NAMES are reported and values never are: discovery reads which keys exist, never what they contain.

| Parameter                                  | Type   | Description                                                       |
| ------------------------------------------ | ------ | ----------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `source` <span class="req">required</span> | string | Adoption source uuid, from list-adoption-sources.                 |
| `organization`                             | string | Organisation uuid or slug. Omit to use your default organisation. |

### `migrate-adoption-data`

<p class="tool-meta">Tier <code>mcp:read</code> · permission <code>deployments.update.item</code></p>

Copy a discovered application's DATA onto the G8Deck application that replaces it: its MySQL/MariaDB database (dumped on the source with the credentials in its own .env, imported as the target server's admin into the database attach-application-database created) and the directories it writes to (paths relative to the discovered root, e.g. storage/app, extracted into the application's shared/ tree so every release sees them, owned by the application's own account, mtimes kept). dry_run defaults to TRUE and writes nothing: it returns the plan — source database, engine, size and table count as discovered; the target database and every table it would REPLACE; each path's bytes and file count on the source and what already sits at its target. dry_run: false queues the copy and returns a run uuid for get-adoption-data-migration. A run REPLACES the target: existing tables are dropped first and each target path is replaced, so running it again is the final sync at cutover. It verifies exact row counts per table and file counts and bytes per path on both sides — a mismatch fails the run (on a live source the counts move; pass put_source_in_maintenance: true on the final sync to run `php artisan down` on the source first). Nothing else on the source is changed; temp files live in a private directory that is always removed. Credentials and row data never cross this boundary — the response carries names, counts and sizes only. PostgreSQL sources are refused, as are remote databases (a reference, not a migration) and paths outside the application's shared directories.

| Parameter                                       | Type            | Description                                                                                                                                                                                          |
| ----------------------------------------------- | --------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `source` <span class="req">required</span>      | string          | Adoption source uuid, from list-adoption-sources.                                                                                                                                                    |
| `application` <span class="req">required</span> | string          | Discovered application uuid, from get-adoption-source.                                                                                                                                               |
| `workload` <span class="req">required</span>    | string          | The G8Deck application (deployment workload) uuid that replaces it. Its database must already exist (attach-application-database).                                                                   |
| `database`                                      | boolean         | Copy the application's database. Default true.                                                                                                                                                       |
| `paths`                                         | array of string | Directories relative to the discovered application root, e.g. ["storage/app", "storage/media"]. No absolute paths, no "..". Each must sit inside a directory the application shares across releases. |
| `dry_run`                                       | boolean         | Default TRUE: report the plan and write nothing. false queues the copy (needs an mcp:write token).                                                                                                   |
| `put_source_in_maintenance`                     | boolean         | Run `php artisan down` on the source before dumping — for the final sync at cutover. Default false. The source stays down afterwards.                                                                |
| `organization`                                  | string          | Organisation uuid or slug. Omit to use your default organisation.                                                                                                                                    |

### `get-adoption-data-migration`

<p class="tool-meta">Tier <code>mcp:read</code> · permission <code>migration-sources.view.list</code></p>

Read one migrate-adoption-data run: status (pending, running, succeeded, failed), the phase it reached, the plan it was queued with, and its report — per table row counts on source and target with any mismatches, and per path bytes and file counts before and after. failure_reason says why a run stopped. Names and counts only; never a credential or a row.

| Parameter                               | Type   | Description                                                       |
| --------------------------------------- | ------ | ----------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `run` <span class="req">required</span> | string | Run uuid returned by migrate-adoption-data.                       |
| `organization`                          | string | Organisation uuid or slug. Omit to use your default organisation. |

### `list-database-servers`

<p class="tool-meta">Tier <code>mcp:read</code> · permission <code>database-servers.view.list</code></p>

The database daemons G8Deck administers for this organisation: engine, endpoint, TLS, whether it was adopted or installed, and how many databases and users it carries. `node` is null when the machine underneath has been retired — such a server administers nothing and is a stale record, which is what withdraw-database-server clears. Stored admin credentials never cross this boundary.

| Parameter      | Type    | Description                                                                                              |
| -------------- | ------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `node`         | string  | Only servers on this managed node uuid, from list-managed-nodes.                                         |
| `orphaned`     | boolean | Only servers whose managed node no longer exists — stale records left behind when a machine was retired. |
| `organization` | string  | Organisation uuid or slug. Omit to use your default organisation.                                        |
| `page`         | integer | Page number, starting at 1.                                                                              |
| `per_page`     | integer | Results per page, 1-100 (default 20).                                                                    |

### `list-managed-databases`

<p class="tool-meta">Tier <code>mcp:read</code> · permission <code>database-servers.view.list</code></p>

What is INSIDE one managed database server: its databases, its login roles and which role holds which privilege on which database. `status` is per record and means the daemon: `pending` is recorded but not yet confirmed by the daemon, `active` is converged, `failed` carries `last_error`. Stored passwords never cross this boundary — a user reports its name, its status and whether a credential is held, never the value. A dropped name stays reserved on its server, so a create refused as "already exists" may be naming a database nobody can see.

| Parameter                                           | Type   | Description                                                       |
| --------------------------------------------------- | ------ | ----------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `database_server` <span class="req">required</span> | string | Database server uuid, from list-database-servers.                 |
| `organization`                                      | string | Organisation uuid or slug. Omit to use your default organisation. |

### `list-database-extensions`

<p class="tool-meta">Tier <code>mcp:read</code> · permission <code>database-servers.view.list</code></p>

PostgreSQL extensions on one managed database server — three different facts, kept apart. `catalogue` is what G8Deck offers and what enable-database-extension accepts. `available` is what the DAEMON can load, read from the machine: it is per server, and an empty list means nothing is installed while `available_error` means nobody could look — never read one as the other. `databases[].extensions` is what is actually enabled in each database, per record: `pending` is recorded but unconfirmed, `active` is in the database, and `failed` carries the machine's own words in `last_error` — including the RHEL-family refusal, which is a deliberate refusal with a reason rather than a package name guessed wrong. Extensions are a PostgreSQL capability; on any other engine this reports that and nothing else.

| Parameter                                           | Type   | Description                                                       |
| --------------------------------------------------- | ------ | ----------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `database_server` <span class="req">required</span> | string | Database server uuid, from list-database-servers.                 |
| `organization`                                      | string | Organisation uuid or slug. Omit to use your default organisation. |

### `get-database-cluster`

<p class="tool-meta">Tier <code>mcp:read</code> · permission <code>database-servers.view.list</code></p>

The replication cluster a database server belongs to: every member with its role (primary or replica), lifecycle status, health and replication reading. Name any member. A standalone server answers `cluster: null` with itself as the only member. Replication readings keep four answers apart and never flatten them: `never_probed` (no reading at all), `unknown`/`stale` health (the probe could not be taken, or is too old), `unreachable` (the daemon did not answer, so replication has no reading), and a `replication.state` — primary, streaming, disconnected, unexpected_writer, unexpected_standby, or undetermined (the daemon answered but replication could not be read). `lag_seconds` is null when unknown, never 0 by default. Applications and backups always use the member with role primary.

| Parameter                                           | Type   | Description                                                       |
| --------------------------------------------------- | ------ | ----------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `database_server` <span class="req">required</span> | string | Any member's database server uuid, from list-database-servers.    |
| `organization`                                      | string | Organisation uuid or slug. Omit to use your default organisation. |

### `list-storage-buckets`

<p class="tool-meta">Tier <code>mcp:read</code> · permission <code>storage-servers.view.list</code></p>

The organisation's managed object storage buckets: which storage server each is on, its status, its quotas, and which deployment and application (if any) is attached to it. A bucket with no attachment still holds every object ever written to it — detaching an application never deletes data. Access key secrets and ids never cross this boundary.

| Parameter      | Type    | Description                                                                                                                 |
| -------------- | ------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `server`       | string  | Only buckets on this storage server uuid.                                                                                   |
| `attached`     | boolean | true for buckets an application is wired to, false for those with no attachment. A detached bucket still holds its objects. |
| `organization` | string  | Organisation uuid or slug. Omit to use your default organisation.                                                           |
| `page`         | integer | Page number, starting at 1.                                                                                                 |
| `per_page`     | integer | Results per page, 1-100 (default 20).                                                                                       |

### `get-storage-cluster`

<p class="tool-meta">Tier <code>mcp:read</code> · permission <code>storage-servers.view.list</code></p>

One managed storage server's cluster: the primary node and every additional member, each node's zone, capacity and recorded status, the replication factor and whether it is redundant, the S3 backends any client or load balancer can use, and a LIVE health reading taken now over SSH from the primary. Cluster state is healthy, degraded (a node in the layout is unreachable), not_serving (no node holds a layout role), unreachable (the daemon said no) or unknown (the reading could not be taken — never read that as down). Per node: healthy, failed, absent (not in the cluster) or unknown.

| Parameter                                          | Type   | Description                                                       |
| -------------------------------------------------- | ------ | ----------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `storage_server` <span class="req">required</span> | string | Storage server uuid, from list-storage-buckets.                   |
| `organization`                                     | string | Organisation uuid or slug. Omit to use your default organisation. |

### `get-billable-hosts`

<p class="tool-meta">Tier <code>mcp:read</code> · permission <code>quotas.manage.item</code> · organisation owner or administrator only</p>

Billable host counts per provider. For cluster-style providers this is the STORED count refreshed by g8deck:count-billable-hosts — never a live call, and never a fallback to counting node rows, which would bill fifty containers on one daemon like fifty machines.

| Parameter      | Type   | Description                                                       |
| -------------- | ------ | ----------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `organization` | string | Organisation uuid or slug. Omit to use your default organisation. |

<p class="tool-meta">Tier <code>mcp:read</code> · permission <code>quotas.manage.item</code> · organisation owner or administrator only</p>

One organisation's billing position: the agreement in force (plan, stored status, derived entitlement state, trial or period dates, scheduled downgrade, do-not-renew), any checkout awaiting payment, the outstanding invoices, and whether billing and self-serve are switched on. Read-only — no tool on any server moves money or changes an agreement; those stay behind a page.

| Parameter      | Type   | Description                                                       |

| `organization` | string | Organisation uuid or slug. Omit to use your default organisation. |

Bootstrap templates visible to this organisation — the platform catalogue plus any the organisation owns.

<p class="tool-meta">Tier <code>mcp:read</code> · permission <code>infra-providers.view.list</code></p>

Node bootstrap jobs for this organisation's providers, newest first.

| Parameter      | Type    | Description                                                                                                |
| -------------- | ------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `status`       | string  | Filter by bootstrap status. One of: `pending`, `connecting`, `installing`, `verifying`, `ready`, `failed`. |

### `get-bootstrap-job`

<p class="tool-meta">Tier <code>mcp:read</code> · permission <code>infra-providers.view.list</code></p>

One bootstrap job in full: target address, detected OS family, the step log, and any error. The detected OS is a fact read from /etc/os-release, not the dropdown an operator picked — a family mismatch fails the run before the credential rotation, so a wrong template costs nothing.

| Parameter                               | Type   | Description                                                       |
| --------------------------------------- | ------ | ----------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `job` <span class="req">required</span> | string | Bootstrap job uuid.                                               |
| `organization`                          | string | Organisation uuid or slug. Omit to use your default organisation. |

### `get-patch-policy`

<p class="tool-meta">Tier <code>mcp:read</code> · permission <code>infra-providers.view.list</code></p>

The organisation's patch policy: mode (automatic — the default — notify_only or manual), scope (security or all), the maintenance window (ISO weekdays 1=Monday…7=Sunday, start and end HH:MM, timezone; an end before the start wraps midnight) and whether it is open now, allow_disruptive_restarts, critical_outside_window (used by advisories), and the extra contacts (emails; whether a webhook is set — never its URL). Each server lists its patch_policy_override (null inherits) and its effective_mode — the stricter of the two — plus scheduled (whether the scheduler will actually patch it) and excluded_reason when it will not: adopted (another panel owns its packages), the control plane (patched by an operator), protected, unreachable, or a policy that is not automatic. In automatic mode the scheduler patches os-security and every installed runtime/service inside the window, one target at a time, through patch-fleet's canary and halt; adopted servers and the control plane are never patched by the scheduler.

| Parameter      | Type   | Description                                                       |
| -------------- | ------ | ----------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `organization` | string | Organisation uuid or slug. Omit to use your default organisation. |

### `list-advisories`

<p class="tool-meta">Tier <code>mcp:read</code> · permission <code>mcp.access.cross-tenant</code></p>

Every published security advisory, newest first, with an exposure summary per organisation (exposed / fixed / not_exploitable_here / unknown — always all four) and its notice state (notified, escalated, postponements, assessment, critical run, SLA evidence). `still_exposed` is the ops escalation list: critical advisories with servers still exposed 24 hours or more after the organisation was told. Ops only (mcp.access.cross-tenant).

| Parameter | Type    | Description                            |
| --------- | ------- | -------------------------------------- |
| `target`  | string  | Only advisories for this patch target. |
| `limit`   | integer | Newest N advisories (default 25).      |

### `get-advisory-exposure`

<p class="tool-meta">Tier <code>mcp:read</code> · permission <code>mcp.access.cross-tenant</code></p>

Per-server exposure to one advisory: state (exposed, fixed, not_exploitable_here, unknown — four, never collapsed; unknown is never fixed), why, the recorded versions it was judged on with recorded_at and the run outcome they came from (recorded: false = nothing was ever read, run patch-fleet for the target), and whether the scheduler will patch that server (scheduled, excluded_reason — adopted servers and the control plane never are). One organisation with `organization`, otherwise every organisation with a server. Ops only (mcp.access.cross-tenant).

| Parameter                                    | Type   | Description                                                           |
| -------------------------------------------- | ------ | --------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `advisory` <span class="req">required</span> | string | Advisory uuid (from list-advisories).                                 |
| `organization`                               | string | Organisation uuid or slug. Omit for every organisation with a server. |

### `list-registries`

<p class="tool-meta">Tier <code>mcp:read</code> · permission <code>registries.view.list</code></p>

Container registries configured for this organisation. Credentials are never returned — only whether the registry is active.

| Parameter      | Type   | Description                                                       |
| -------------- | ------ | ----------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `organization` | string | Organisation uuid or slug. Omit to use your default organisation. |

### `list-git-credentials`

<p class="tool-meta">Tier <code>mcp:read</code> · permission <code>git-credentials.view.list</code></p>

Git credentials configured for this organisation: the HTTPS host each one authenticates, whether a token and a pinned SSH host key are stored, and whether it is active. The token itself and the username are never returned. A repository whose host has no active credential clones anonymously; SSH repository URLs use a per-application deploy key instead.

| Parameter      | Type   | Description                                                       |
| -------------- | ------ | ----------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `organization` | string | Organisation uuid or slug. Omit to use your default organisation. |

### `list-quotas`

<p class="tool-meta">Tier <code>mcp:read</code> · permission <code>quotas.view.own</code></p>

Resource quotas in this organisation, at every scope — or, for a caller who is not its owner or an administrator, only the quotas that bind them (their own, their teams', the organisation's). IMPORTANT: 0 means "does not constrain at this scope", not "zero allowed" — resolution walks user, then team, then organisation and takes the first non-zero value per field, so a field nobody sets is unlimited. `max_deployments` is labelled "App environments" in the UI: it caps places (one application in one environment), never deploys or releases, and counts neither deleted deployments nor failed launches that hold no servers.

| Parameter      | Type   | Description                                                       |
| -------------- | ------ | ----------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `organization` | string | Organisation uuid or slug. Omit to use your default organisation. |

### `get-usage-summary`

<p class="tool-meta">Tier <code>mcp:read</code> · permission <code>quotas.view.own</code></p>

Rolled-up consumption for this organisation by period. CPU and memory are hour-weighted; storage is a PEAK, not a sum — it is a level rather than a rate, and summing it would bill the same disk once per sample.

| Parameter      | Type    | Description                                                       |
| -------------- | ------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `periods`      | integer | How many recent periods to return, 1-24 (default 6).              |
| `organization` | string  | Organisation uuid or slug. Omit to use your default organisation. |

### `system-health`

<p class="tool-meta">Tier <code>mcp:read</code> · permission <code>admin.view.panel</code></p>

Control-plane health: queue depth and stuck jobs, failed jobs, the scheduler heartbeat, and the mail transport actually in force. Answers "is anything going to run at all" before you spend time on why one deployment did not.

| Parameter      | Type   | Description                                                                                              |
| -------------- | ------ | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `organization` | string | Organisation uuid or slug, used for the provider preflight check. Omit to use your default organisation. |

## Write tools

### `update-infra-provider`

<p class="tool-meta">Tier <code>mcp:write</code> · permission <code>infra-providers.update.item</code> · organisation owner or administrator only</p>

Correct a provider's bookkeeping: name, location, whether it is active, and the protection lock. Takes final values, not deltas — omitted fields are left alone — and reports exactly which fields moved. Credentials and provider type are NOT editable here: credential values never cross this boundary, and the type decides the credential schema. Adding the protection lock is allowed; removing it is refused.

| Parameter                                    | Type    | Description                                                                                                                                      |
| -------------------------------------------- | ------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| `provider` <span class="req">required</span> | string  | Provider uuid. Must belong to your organisation. Providers have no slug.                                                                         |
| `name`                                       | string  | New display name, 2-120 characters. Omit to leave it alone.                                                                                      |
| `location`                                   | string  | Region or site label. Pass an empty string to clear it; omit to leave it alone.                                                                  |
| `is_active`                                  | boolean | Whether the scheduler may place new work here. Existing deployments are unaffected either way.                                                   |
| `is_protected`                               | boolean | The lock that refuses bootstrap, reconfiguration and teardown. May be set to true here; setting it to false is refused — unlock in the web form. |
| `protection_reason`                          | string  | Required whenever the lock is on. Quoted back to whoever hits the refusal, so write it for them.                                                 |
| `organization`                               | string  | Organisation uuid or slug. Omit to use your default organisation.                                                                                |

### `trust-host-key`

<p class="tool-meta">Tier <code>mcp:write</code> · permission <code>infra-providers.update.item</code> · organisation owner or administrator only</p>

Re-pin the SSH host key G8Deck trusts for a provider, after the machine behind it was legitimately rebuilt. The fingerprint you pass is compared against the one the host actually presents before anything is stored: a typo, or a key you were not expecting, is refused rather than trusted. Node rows at the same address are re-pinned too. This never clears a pin — there is no way to say 'trust whatever answers'.

| Parameter                                       | Type    | Description                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                           |
| ----------------------------------------------- | ------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `provider` <span class="req">required</span>    | string  | Provider uuid. Must belong to your organisation and speak SSH.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        |
| `fingerprint` <span class="req">required</span> | string  | The host key you mean to trust, in OpenSSH form (SHA256:…). It is compared against what the host presents; a mismatch is refused, so this must come from somewhere you verified — the machine's console, ssh-keygen -lf, or the "got …" half of a host key mismatch. There is no way to say "trust whatever answers". |
| `host`                                          | string  | Address to probe. Omit to use the provider's own SSH host.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            |
| `port`                                          | integer | SSH port. Omit to use the provider's own.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                             |
| `organization`                                  | string  | Organisation uuid or slug. Omit to use your default organisation.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                     |

### `test-provider-connection`

<p class="tool-meta">Tier <code>mcp:write</code> · permission <code>infra-providers.test.connection</code> · organisation owner or administrator only</p>

Queue a connection test against a provider. The result lands on the provider record — read it back with get-infra-provider once a worker has run the job.

| Parameter                                    | Type   | Description                                                       |
| -------------------------------------------- | ------ | ----------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `provider` <span class="req">required</span> | string | Provider uuid.                                                    |
| `organization`                               | string | Organisation uuid or slug. Omit to use your default organisation. |

### `run-adoption-sweep`

<p class="tool-meta">Tier <code>mcp:write</code> · permission <code>migration-sources.run.discovery</code> · organisation owner or administrator only</p>

Queue a read-only sweep of an inventoried server. It writes NOTHING to the machine — the adapter interface has no write methods, and every command it ran is recorded so the claim can be checked. The sweep runs on the infra queue under Horizon, so the inventory is not ready when this returns; read it back with get-adoption-source. It replaces the previous inventory rather than adding to it, so an application removed from the machine disappears here too. Decisions already taken on rows that are found again are NOT preserved — re-sweeping resets them.

| Parameter                                  | Type   | Description                                                       |
| ------------------------------------------ | ------ | ----------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `source` <span class="req">required</span> | string | Adoption source uuid, from list-adoption-sources.                 |
| `organization`                             | string | Organisation uuid or slug. Omit to use your default organisation. |

### `decide-adoption-item`

<p class="tool-meta">Tier <code>mcp:write</code> · permission <code>migration-sources.decide.items</code> · organisation owner or administrator only</p>

Mark one discovered application or database adopt / skip / replace. This is what a later cutover acts on, so it is a decision, not a label: Undecided is the default and stays the default, because silence must not read as consent. On the first fleet swept, three of ten applications were Skip — one dead, two replaced by a rewrite. A REMOTE database cannot be marked adopt: it is a reference the application keeps pointing at, and "adopt" here means move the data.

| Parameter                                    | Type   | Description                                                                                                                        |
| -------------------------------------------- | ------ | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `source` <span class="req">required</span>   | string | Adoption source uuid.                                                                                                              |
| `item` <span class="req">required</span>     | string | Uuid of the discovered application or database, from get-adoption-source.                                                          |
| `decision` <span class="req">required</span> | string | adopt — bring it across as it is; skip — leave it behind; replace — something new takes its place; undecided — clear the decision. |
| `organization`                               | string | Organisation uuid or slug. Omit to use your default organisation.                                                                  |

### `adopt-discovered-server`

<p class="tool-meta">Tier <code>mcp:write</code> · permission <code>migration-sources.adopt.node</code> · organisation owner or administrator only</p>

Register an inventoried machine as a managed server. It reads the login, `hostname` and /etc/os-release, and installs G8Deck's node tooling: the metrics collector — a POSIX sh script, a systemd service, a timer and an env file — and the sqlite3 CLI plus its headers, one package-manager run. Both because the only other installer is the bootstrap pipeline, which rewrites the firewall and SSH access of a machine that is already serving: a fleet entry that can never report a reading is not really in the fleet, and a server with no sqlite3 cannot have any SQLite file on it checked or backed up. Pass metrics=false to skip BOTH, leaving the machine completely untouched — the field keeps its name because renaming a published tool surface breaks clients, but it is one consent for both installs. Nothing else is installed: no firewall change, no credential rotation. The old panel keeps serving every application, keeps its cron and keeps renewing its certificates — standing it down is a separate, later, explicit act. The node is recorded with no stack version and no bootstrapped_at, because G8Deck bootstrapped nothing, and the hourly inventory refresh will not write its manifest there while the source row exists. Refused for a machine nobody has swept, for this control plane, and for a server G8Deck itself set up. Reversible: retire the node, and the collector and the two packages are the only things to remove.

| Parameter                                  | Type    | Description                                                                                                                                                   |
| ------------------------------------------ | ------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `source` <span class="req">required</span> | string  | Adoption source uuid, from list-adoption-sources. It must have been swept.                                                                                    |
| `metrics`                                  | boolean | Install the metrics collector (default true). False leaves the machine completely untouched — and the server then reports no readings until one is installed. |
| `organization`                             | string  | Organisation uuid or slug. Omit to use your default organisation.                                                                                             |

### `import-adoption-env`

<p class="tool-meta">Tier <code>mcp:write</code> · permission <code>deployments.update.item</code></p>

Read a discovered application's .env off the source machine and write it into the G8Deck application that replaces it. This is the ONE place those values are read — discovery records key names and never values, so that a hundred-key .env full of root passwords and cloud credentials never sits in our database waiting for approval. Values travel INBOUND ONLY: the response names each key and what happened to it (added, changed, unchanged, refused, skipped) and never echoes a value. Two sets of keys are skipped by default — what the new machine owns (DB__, REDIS__, APP_KEY, APP_URL), because copying them points the migrated application back at the server it was leaving, and what the build recipe manages in production (APP_ENV, APP_DEBUG), because a .env carrying APP_DEBUG=true would put the first live deploy into debug mode. Pass `carry` to bring a skipped key across deliberately — APP_KEY is the usual one, since a fresh key cannot read a single encrypted column. Merges rather than replaces, and applies on the NEXT deploy.

| Parameter                                       | Type   | Description                                                                                                      |
| ----------------------------------------------- | ------ | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `source` <span class="req">required</span>      | string | Adoption source uuid, from list-adoption-sources.                                                                |
| `application` <span class="req">required</span> | string | Discovered application uuid, from get-adoption-source.                                                           |
| `workload` <span class="req">required</span>    | string | The G8Deck application (deployment workload) uuid to write the environment into.                                 |
| `carry`                                         | array  | Skipped, target-owned keys to import anyway — APP_KEY, APP_URL, DB__, REDIS__. Name only what you mean to carry. |
| `organization`                                  | string | Organisation uuid or slug. Omit to use your default organisation.                                                |

### `create-managed-database`

<p class="tool-meta">Tier <code>mcp:write</code> · permission <code>database-servers.manage.databases</code> · organisation owner or administrator only</p>

Create a database on a managed server. The record is written first with status `pending` — recorded, but the daemon has not confirmed it — and a job then creates it for real; read the outcome back with list-managed-databases. The name is validated against the server's ENGINE, not a generic rule: `mysql` is the account table on a MySQL server and an ordinary name on a PostgreSQL one. A dropped name stays reserved on its server, so "already exists" can name a database nobody can see any more. Creating a database grants nobody access to it — use grant-database-access.

| Parameter                                           | Type   | Description                                                                                                                                                          |
| --------------------------------------------------- | ------ | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `database_server` <span class="req">required</span> | string | Database server uuid, from list-database-servers.                                                                                                                    |
| `name` <span class="req">required</span>            | string | The database name. Validated against the server's engine; names reserved by the engine and names already used on this server — including dropped ones — are refused. |
| `organization`                                      | string | Organisation uuid or slug. Omit to use your default organisation.                                                                                                    |

### `create-database-user`

<p class="tool-meta">Tier <code>mcp:write</code> · permission <code>database-servers.manage.users</code> · organisation owner or administrator only</p>

Create a login role on a managed database server. The password is GENERATED where it is stored and is never returned here — a password that crosses this boundary has been in a transcript, which is the same rule set-workload-env follows. Read it back on the server's page in G8Deck, behind the database-servers.reveal.credentials permission, where the reveal is audited. The username is validated against the server's engine: `root` is sacred on MySQL, `postgres` on PostgreSQL, and only the MySQL family caps a name at 32 characters. A dropped username stays reserved on its server. The new role reaches no database until grant-database-access says which.

| Parameter                                           | Type   | Description                                                                                                                                                                                                |
| --------------------------------------------------- | ------ | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `database_server` <span class="req">required</span> | string | Database server uuid, from list-database-servers.                                                                                                                                                          |
| `username` <span class="req">required</span>        | string | The login role name. Validated against the server's engine; engine-reserved names and names already used on this server — including dropped ones — are refused. No password is accepted: one is generated. |
| `organization`                                      | string | Organisation uuid or slug. Omit to use your default organisation.                                                                                                                                          |

### `grant-database-access`

<p class="tool-meta">Tier <code>mcp:write</code> · permission <code>database-servers.manage.databases</code> · organisation owner or administrator only</p>

Give one login role one privilege preset on one database. There is ONE privilege per (database, user) pair: granting again REPLACES what the role held rather than adding to it, so re-granting read_only to a role that had read_write takes write access away. Presets are read_only, read_write and owner. The database and the user must be on the same server — a cross-server pair is refused and the refusal is audited, because the daemon-side grant would land on one machine for a role recorded against another. Queued: `status` stays pending until the daemon converges.

| Parameter                                            | Type   | Description                                                                                     |
| ---------------------------------------------------- | ------ | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `database_server` <span class="req">required</span>  | string | Database server uuid, from list-database-servers. The database and the user must both be on it. |
| `managed_database` <span class="req">required</span> | string | Managed database uuid, from list-managed-databases.                                             |
| `database_user` <span class="req">required</span>    | string | Database user uuid, from list-managed-databases.                                                |
| `privilege` <span class="req">required</span>        | string | read_only, read_write or owner. It REPLACES whatever this role held on this database.           |
| `organization`                                       | string | Organisation uuid or slug. Omit to use your default organisation.                               |

### `revoke-database-access`

<p class="tool-meta">Tier <code>mcp:write</code> · permission <code>database-servers.manage.databases</code> · organisation owner or administrator only</p>

Withdraw one login role's access to one database. It deletes no data and drops no role: what goes is the grant. It is mcp:write and takes no retyped confirmation, because withdrawing access is not taking infrastructure apart — but it IS disruptive, and an application connecting as this role starts being refused at its next query. The grant row is removed outright so the pair can be re-granted immediately, and the daemon converges after. Refused when the role holds no grant on that database, rather than reported as a no-op.

| Parameter                                            | Type   | Description                                                       |
| ---------------------------------------------------- | ------ | ----------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `database_server` <span class="req">required</span>  | string | Database server uuid, from list-database-servers.                 |
| `managed_database` <span class="req">required</span> | string | Managed database uuid, from list-managed-databases.               |
| `database_user` <span class="req">required</span>    | string | Database user uuid, from list-managed-databases.                  |
| `organization`                                       | string | Organisation uuid or slug. Omit to use your default organisation. |

### `enable-database-extension`

<p class="tool-meta">Tier <code>mcp:write</code> · permission <code>database-servers.manage.databases</code> · organisation owner or administrator only</p>

Enable a PostgreSQL extension in ONE database. Two halves run in order and fail separately: the OS package is installed on the SERVER (shared by every database on that daemon, skipped when it is already there), then `CREATE EXTENSION` runs in THIS database and does nothing for the next one. The record is written `pending` and a job does both — read it back with list-database-extensions, where a `failed` row carries the machine's own reason. One of those reasons is a refusal rather than a fault: on the RHEL family G8Deck declines to name a package, because PGDG's build belongs to PGDG's own PostgreSQL installation and the AppStream daemon would never read it — an install that reported success and left CREATE EXTENSION answering "not available" is worse than the sentence you get instead.

| Parameter                                            | Type   | Description                                                                                                                                                                                                                                           |
| ---------------------------------------------------- | ------ | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `database_server` <span class="req">required</span>  | string | Database server uuid, from list-database-servers. Must run PostgreSQL.                                                                                                                                                                                |
| `managed_database` <span class="req">required</span> | string | The database uuid to enable it in, from list-managed-databases or list-database-extensions.                                                                                                                                                           |
| `extension` <span class="req">required</span>        | string | One of the catalogue names from list-database-extensions: `vector` (pgvector) or `postgis`. Nothing else is accepted — the package that provides each one is per OS family and per major, and a name G8Deck does not carry has no package to install. |
| `organization`                                       | string | Organisation uuid or slug. Omit to use your default organisation.                                                                                                                                                                                     |

### `disable-database-extension`

<p class="tool-meta">Tier <code>mcp:write</code> · permission <code>database-servers.manage.databases</code> · organisation owner or administrator only</p>

Queue `DROP EXTENSION` in one database. It deletes no data and drops no role: **G8Deck never passes CASCADE, and there is no argument that makes it.** The daemon refuses while any column still uses the type, and that refusal is the correct outcome — CASCADE would make the drop succeed by deleting the customer's columns. The refusal reaches the record verbatim ("column embedding of table items depends on type vector" is a better message than anything written here) and the next step is in the application, not on this server.
